title: Are Household Incomes Keeping Up With Grocery Prices?
text:
Higher grocery bills do not automatically mean that food has become more expensive relative to other goods, or that incomes buy less food. Those comparisons require a benchmark. This post asks: How did U.S. grocery prices change relative to overall consumer prices and median household income between 2015 and 2024, and how does the answer differ since 2020?
I use monthly, seasonally adjusted BLS consumer price indexes and annual Census median household income in current dollars. The code first tries FRED and, if unavailable, downloads from the official BLS API and Census H-5 table. Each saved series records its actual source; the Census fallback uses published rounded current-dollar values. Monthly indexes are averaged within each calendar year; 2014 observations supply the twelve-month lag for 2015 inflation. All annual comparisons end in 2024. The code saves downloads and calculated results, checks for missing months, and reuses saved data on subsequent renders.

title: Are Our Paychecks Keeping Up With Food Prices?
section: Food became more expensive—but the relative price matters
text:
Food became more expensive—but the relative price matters









Both food-at-home prices and the overall consumer price level increased. Before 2020, food-at-home prices generally increased more slowly than overall consumer prices. After 2020, food prices accelerated and moved slightly above the overall CPI. The important point is, not simply that prices increased, but food became relatively more expensive compared with the overall consumer price level.
To measure this relative-price difference, I subtract the All Items CPI from the Food-at-Home CPI after indexing both series to 2020 = 100:









The relative-price gap became positive after 2020 and was largest around 2022. A positive gap means that food prices had increased more than overall consumer prices relative to 2020. (This is a difference in cumulative price levels, not a difference in annual inflation rates.)
The overall food inflation rate provides a more detailed view of how this inflation episode evolved over time：









Food-at-Home inflation accelerated sharply during 2022 and then declined substantially in 2023. This highlights an important distinction between inflation and the price level: a lower inflation rate means that food prices are rising more slowly, not that they are falling. Thus, even after food inflation cooled, households could continue to face a higher food-price level than before the inflation surge.

title: Are Our Paychecks Keeping Up With Food Prices?
section: What Is Happening Inside the Grocery Basket? Not All Food Inflation Is the Same
text:
What Is Happening Inside the Grocery Basket? Not All Food Inflation Is the Same
Food includes many different products, and their prices did not move together. From 2015 to 2024, the five selected food categories—cereals and bakery products, meats, poultry, fish and eggs, fruits and vegetables, nonalcoholic beverages, and dairy products—experienced noticeably different cumulative price increases.









This matters because aggregate food inflation can hide differences across consumption baskets. A household that spends more on a rapidly increasing category may face greater food-price pressure than a household whose purchases are concentrated in slower-growing categories.
The timing of these price increases also matters. Annual price growth accelerated around 2021–2022, but the magnitude and timing varied across categories:









These differences show that food inflation was not a uniform shock across products. Different categories experienced stronger price increases at different times, so households with different consumption patterns could experience different rates of food-price growth.

title: Are Our Paychecks Keeping Up With Food Prices?
text:
Did Income Keep Up?
Price increases become more meaningful when compared with household income. I normalize median household income and the Food-at-Home CPI to 2020 = 100：









Before 2020, median household income generally grew faster than food prices. During 2021–2022, food prices temporarily grew faster than income, increasing the cost of food relative to median household income. By 2024, the two measures had moved closer together.
To summarize this relationship, I construct a Food Purchasing-Power Index:
\[
\text{Food Purchasing-Power Index}_t
=
\frac{\text{Income Index}_t}
{\text{Food Price Index}_t}
\times 100
\]
The index is normalized to 100 in 2020.

A value above 100 means income increased faster than food prices relative to 2020.
A value below 100 means food prices increased faster than income.
A value of 100 means the two grew proportionally relative to the base year.










The index rose from about 86 in 2015 to above 100 before the pandemic, fell to roughly 95 in 2022, and recovered toward 100 by 2024.
The result is more nuanced than saying that households permanently lost purchasing power. The food-price shock temporarily reduced median income relative to food prices, but this gap narrowed as income continued to grow and food inflation slowed.

title: Are Household Incomes Keeping Up With Grocery Prices?
text:
Takeaway
The starting year matters. Grocery prices rose in dollars, but their relative price decreased by 4.4% over the full 2015–2024 window, versus increased by 1.1% since 2020. Food purchasing power likewise requires an explicit comparison period. Reading relative prices, inflation rates, and income together explains why easing inflation need not bring either lower grocery bills or the same experience for every household.

title: Value or Value‑Trap? Identifying Risks in US Small‑Mid‑Cap Stocks via Web‑Scraped Finviz Data
text: Disclaimer: This educational analysis is for class demonstration only and does not constitute investment advice. All findings are descriptive statistics derived from a limited public sample dataset and must not be used for live trading.

title: Value or Value‑Trap? Identifying Risks in US Small‑Mid‑Cap Stocks via Web‑Scraped Finviz Data
text:
1. Introduction and Research Questions
The price‑to‑earnings (P/E) ratio is one of the most accessible valuation metrics for retail investors. Many retail stock screeners treat a low P/E as a straightforward signal that a stock is cheap and worth buying. However, a low P/E is ambiguous: it can signal genuine undervaluation, or it can mark a value trap.
A value‑trap describes securities that appear cheap based on headline multiples, where low valuations already price in expected future fundamental deterioration. Professional institutional investors have access to more thorough due‑diligence resources. Widespread institutional selling combined with elevated short interest often signals deteriorating profit outlooks. Compared with large‑cap equities, small‑mid‑cap stocks suffer from lower information transparency, leaving retail investors especially vulnerable to value‑trap risks.
This study uses the rvest package to scrape static HTML tables from Finviz and addresses two empirical questions: 1. Among US small‑mid‑cap stocks, which sectors combine low median P/E ratios with relatively high institutional ownership? These sectors may represent value opportunities still endorsed by professional investors. 2. Which sectors exhibit the joint pattern of low P/E, low institutional ownership, and high short interest? Such sectors carry elevated value‑trap risks for retail participants.

Ethical Scraping Statement This project scrapes only publicly‑available static HTML tables from Finviz. No login‑restricted or private content is accessed. To mitigate selection bias from default ticker‑alphabetical ordering, we draw samples across multiple sorting dimensions. Reasonable delays are enforced between HTTP requests. In total, 10 web pages are requested exclusively for non‑commercial educational purposes, complying with robots.txt guidelines.

title: Value or Value‑Trap? Identifying Risks in US Small‑Mid‑Cap Stocks via Web‑Scraped Finviz Data
section: 2. Data Collection: Web Scraping Finviz Screener with rvest
text:
2. Data Collection: Web Scraping Finviz Screener with rvest
Scrape data from Finviz screener https://finviz.com/screener via rvest.
Key scraped fields:



Field
Description




ticker
Stock ticker symbol


company_name
Full company name


sector
Industry sector classification


market_cap
Market capitalization


pe
Price‑to‑earnings ratio


institutional_own
Institutional ownership percentage


short_interest
Short interest percentage



Scrape data in RStudio using the following code: Firstly, istall and load packages:
library(rvest)
library(dplyr)
library(purrr)
Checks whether the target folder data/raw already exists. Only if the folder does NOT exist, it creates the nested directory structure data/raw. The recursive = TRUE argument enables creation of parent folders automatically. If the folder already exists, the code does nothing and avoids throwing an error:
if (!dir.exists("data/raw")) {
  dir.create("data/raw", recursive = TRUE)
}
Scrape total 10 page requests (Making sure to be in compliance with ethics) from different pages:
page_sequence <- 1:10
sleep_seconds <-7
scrape_finviz_view <- function(view_code){
  base_url <- paste0("https://finviz.com/screener.ashx?v=", view_code)
  out_df <- tibble()
  
  for(page_num in page_sequence){
    offset <- (page_num - 1L)*20L
    full_url <- paste0(base_url, "&r=", offset)
    message("\nScraping view v=", view_code, " Page ", page_num, " | ", full_url)
    
    page <- read_html(full_url)
    stock_rows <- html_elements(page, css = "tr.styled-row")
    message("Stock rows found: ", length(stock_rows))
    
    page_df <- tibble()
    for(row_node in stock_rows){
      ticker_link <- html_element(row_node, "a[href*='stock?t=']")
      ticker <- if(!is.na(ticker_link)) html_text2(ticker_link) else NA_character_
      
      td_nodes <- html_elements(row_node, "td")
      cell_values <- map_chr(td_nodes, function(td){
        val <- html_attr(td, "data-boxover-value")
        if(is.na(val)) val <- html_text2(td)
        val
      })
      page_df <- bind_rows(page_df, tibble(ticker = ticker, cells = list(cell_values)))
    }
    out_df <- bind_rows(out_df, page_df)
    Sys.sleep(sleep_seconds)
  }
  return(out_df)
}

# v=111 Overview：Ticker,Company,Sector,Industry,Country,MarketCap,P/E
df_v111_raw <- scrape_finviz_view("111")
df_v111 <- df_v111_raw %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(
    company_name = cells[3],
    sector       = cells[4],
    industry     = cells[5],
    country      = cells[6],
    market_cap   = cells[7],
    pe           = cells[8]
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(-cells)

# v=121 Valuation：
df_v121_raw <- scrape_finviz_view("121")
df_v121 <- df_v121_raw %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(
    market_cap_v = cells[3],
    pe_v         = cells[4],
    forward_pe   = cells[5],
    peg          = cells[6],
    ps           = cells[7],
    pb           = cells[8]
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(-cells)

# v=131 Ownership：
df_v131_raw <- scrape_finviz_view("131")
df_v131 <- df_v131_raw %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(
    market_cap_o     = cells[3],
    outstanding      = cells[4],
    float            = cells[5],
    insider_own      = cells[6],
    insider_trans    = cells[7],
    inst_own         = cells[8],
    short_float      = cells[9],
    short_ratio      = cells[10]
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(-cells)

# v=161 Financial：
df_v161_raw <- scrape_finviz_view("161")
df_v161 <- df_v161_raw %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(
    market_cap_f = cells[3],
    roa          = cells[5],
    roe          = cells[6],
    profit_m     = cells[14]
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(-cells)
Merge multiple tables by ticket
combined_all <- df_v111 %>%
  inner_join(df_v121, by = "ticker") %>%
  inner_join(df_v131, by = "ticker") %>%
  inner_join(df_v161, by = "ticker")

write.csv(combined_all, "data/raw/finviz_all_views_raw.csv", row.names = FALSE, na = "")
message("\n✅ Finished scraping. Total merged rows = ", nrow(combined_all))
message("=== preview ===")
print(head(combined_all, 3))

title: Value or Value‑Trap? Identifying Risks in US Small‑Mid‑Cap Stocks via Web‑Scraped Finviz Data
text:
3.Data Cleaning
Clean the data in clean_finviz_all.R.
To kick off, load packages:
library(dplyr)
library(stringr)
Check if the folder ‘data/processed’ exists and automatically create the nested directory if it does not exist:
if (!dir.exists("data/processed")) dir.create("data/processed", recursive = TRUE)
Read the raw dataset:
raw_df <- read.csv("data/raw/finviz_all_views_raw.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
Drop rows with missing critical variables: ticker, P/E, institutional ownership, short float, market capitalization.:
clean_df <- raw_df |>
  filter(!is.na(ticker), ticker != "") |>
  filter(pe != "", inst_own != "", short_float != "", market_cap != "") |>
Strip percentage symbols and convert percentage text fields into numeric values.
  mutate(
    pe_num                     = as.numeric(str_remove(pe, "x")),
    institutional_ownership_pct = as.numeric(str_remove(inst_own, "%")),
    short_float_pct            = as.numeric(str_remove(short_float, "%")),
    roa_num                    = as.numeric(str_remove(roa, "%")),
    roe_num                    = as.numeric(str_remove(roe, "%")),
    profit_margin_pct          = as.numeric(str_remove(profit_m, "%"))
  ) |>
Filter abnormal values of P/E ratio:
  filter(pe_num > 0, pe_num <= 200) |>
Process market value text to generate absolute market value and market value grouping in US dollars:
  mutate(
    market_cap_value = case_when(
      str_ends(market_cap, "B") ~ as.numeric(str_remove(market_cap, "B")) * 1e9,
      str_ends(market_cap, "M") ~ as.numeric(str_remove(market_cap, "M")) * 1e6,
      TRUE ~ NA_real_
    ),
    cap_group = if_else(market_cap_value < 10e9, "Small‑Mid Cap", "Large Cap")
  ) |>
Retain * * sample for research only: small and medium-sized stocks * *; Filter out all large cap stocks to fit the research question of this analysis:
  filter(cap_group == "Small‑Mid Cap") |>
Clean up the industry field, remove the leading and trailing spaces of the string, and remove excess whitespace characters inside:
  mutate(sector = str_squish(sector)) |>
Select the columns , required for the final output dataset and discard any unnecessary original intermediate fields:
  select(
    ticker, company_name, sector, industry, country,
    market_cap, market_cap_value, cap_group,
    pe_num, peg, ps, pb,
    institutional_ownership_pct, short_float_pct,
    roa_num, roe_num, profit_margin_pct
  )
Write the cleaned dataset to the output file, print the number of rows of the cleaned sample, and output the first 6 rows of the dataset for easy visual verification of the cleaning effect during runtime:
write.csv(clean_df, "data/processed/finviz_clean_all.csv", row.names = FALSE, na = "")
message("✅ Clean dataset saved. Rows after clean: ", nrow(clean_df))
print(head(clean_df))

title: Value or Value‑Trap? Identifying Risks in US Small‑Mid‑Cap Stocks via Web‑Scraped Finviz Data
text:
4. Analysis & Visualization



Figure 1


Figure 1 plots sectors by their median P/E ratio and median institutional ownership. Dashed horizontal and vertical lines represent cross‑sector median values, creating four quadrants.

Quadrant: Low‑PE, High institutional ownership (Institution‑approved value sectors)

Sectors falling into this quadrant have below‑sample‑median P/E ratios alongside above‑sample‑median institutional ownership.

For these sectors, low valuation multiples are accompanied by sustained professional investor confidence. Institutional investors have completed deeper due‑diligence; low P/E is more likely driven by price pull‑backs rather than fundamental business deterioration.
These sectors are priority candidates for further fundamental research. A low P/E here is not merely a signal of distress.


Quadrant: Low‑PE, Low institutional ownership (Potential value‑trap sectors)

These sectors display low median P/E but institutions hold comparatively small positions.

Professional market participants have reduced exposure to these industries. The cheap‑looking valuation may reflect market expectations of deteriorating future earnings.
This group represents the core value‑trap risk for retail investors who screen only on P/E alone. Even though stocks appear inexpensive, professional money is voting with reduced holdings.


High‑PE quadrants (remaining sectors)

Sectors with above‑median P/E sit in the upper‑right and bottom‑right quadrants. These are not the focus of our research question: they trade at richer valuations and fall outside our “search‑for‑low‑PE” screening objective.



Figure 2


Figure 2 boxplots compare median short‑interest percentages for:

Institution‑approved low‑PE sectors
Potential value‑trap low‑PE sectors


The potential value‑trap group exhibits materially higher median short‑interest ratios. Higher short interest means more market participants are betting on price declines.
This reinforces the signal from institutional ownership: sectors in the value‑trap quadrant face greater market pessimism.
By contrast, institution‑approved low‑PE sectors show lower typical short interest, consistent with less downside pessimism among market participants.




Figure 3


Figure 3 counts individual small‑mid‑cap firms grouped into PE buckets 0‑10, 10‑20, 20‑50, 50‑200, split by high / low institutional ownership.

Within the cheapest PE bucket (0‑10, very low P/E):

There is a meaningful share of firms belonging to the low‑institutional‑ownership group. This demonstrates an important real‑world fact: many stocks with very low P/E are not backed by institutional investors. If a retail investor blindly selects all stocks with P/E between 0‑10, they automatically get heavy exposure to potential value‑trap candidates.

Moving to moderate‑PE buckets (10‑20, 20‑50):

The proportion of high‑institutional‑ownership firms increases. Many firms with reasonable valuations retain professional investor support.
Key practical takeaway from Figure 3: Very low P/E bins do not consist exclusively of promising value stocks; they contain a substantial pool of stocks shunned by institutional players. Single‑metric screening on P/E is therefore misleading.

title: Value or Value‑Trap? Identifying Risks in US Small‑Mid‑Cap Stocks via Web‑Scraped Finviz Data
text:
5. Key Results & Actionable Takeaways

Synthesized answers to the two research questions
RQ1: Which small‑mid‑cap sectors combine low median P/E with high institutional ownership?
A subset of small‑mid‑cap sectors satisfy both conditions: low sector‑median P/E and above‑median institutional ownership. In our sample, these sectors represent the most plausible value opportunities among low‑P/E names. Professional investors maintain meaningful positions, suggesting the low multiple is more likely to stem from price correction rather than fundamental business decay. These sectors merit deeper fundamental investigation into balance sheets, revenue trends, and profit margins before making investment judgements.
RQ2: Which sectors exhibit low P/E together with low institutional ownership and high short interest (value‑trap risk)?
Another set of sectors in our sample shows low median P/E paired with low institutional ownership and elevated short‑interest percentages. Market professionals have reduced their holdings, and short sellers are positioned for downside moves. These fit the empirical profile of value‑trap sectors. Retail investors relying purely on low P/E would be disproportionately exposed to these high‑risk segments.
Actionable practical insight:
For retail investors screening small‑mid‑cap stocks:

Do not use low P/E as your sole selection criterion.
Prioritize low‑P/E candidates where institutional ownership sits at or above the sample / sector median. This provides auxiliary validation that professionals still trust business fundamentals.
Exrcise heightened caution for stocks or sectors with the triple signal: low P/E, low institutional ownership, high short interest percentage. This combination is a warning sign for potential value traps.
Quntitative screening is only a starting point. Any real‑world investment decision still requires reading financial statements, checking debt levels, and examining revenue dynamics.

title: Value or Value‑Trap? Identifying Risks in US Small‑Mid‑Cap Stocks via Web‑Scraped Finviz Data
text:
6. Limitations

This analysis draws from a small sample (only ten screener pages, 200 lines). Results are descriptive and cannot support strong causal conclusions.
Setor‑level medians can be sensitive to small firm counts within individual industry groups.
Intitutional ownership and short interest are point‑in‑time snapshots; we cannot observe rising / falling ownership trends over time.
P/E itself can be distorted by accounting choices and one‑off profit or loss events.

title: Value or Value‑Trap? Identifying Risks in US Small‑Mid‑Cap Stocks via Web‑Scraped Finviz Data
text:
7.Takeaway
Analytically, low P/E ratios among small‑mid‑cap stocks carry dual meanings: they may indicate promising value opportunities supported by institutional investors, or warn of potential value‑trap risks reflected in low institutional ownership and elevated short interest. Retail investors should avoid single‑metric screening and combine valuation with auxiliary market signals.
From web‑scraping perspective, default ticker‑ordered screener pages introduce substantial selection bias. Multi‑sort sampling can reduce but cannot completely remove such bias. Enforcing reasonable request delays via Sys.sleep() is a core practice for ethical web‑scraping and helps avoid triggering website anti‑scraping restrictions for academic‑scale data collection. Given sampling constraints, all findings are descriptive for educational purposes and cannot substitute real‑world fundamental investment research.

title: Lagrange Multipliers: The Hidden Shadow Prices Behind Constrained Optimization
text: Every economics student learns constrained optimization. Firms maximize profit subject to budget limits; consumers maximize utility subject to income constraints. The Lagrange multiplier method is the standard tool to solve these problems — yet many learners treat it as a mechanical calculus trick without grasping its powerful economic meaning. The multiplier is far more than just an extra variable for taking derivatives: it represents a shadow price, and this interpretation is where most confusion arises.

title: Lagrange Multipliers: The Hidden Shadow Prices Behind Constrained Optimization
text:
Why it feels unintuitive
Calculus classes often teach only the algebra. Students compute first‑order conditions, solve for \(x\) and \(y\), and forget about \(\lambda\). They see \(\lambda\) as a computational nuisance rather than an economically meaningful number. It is easy to mix up its direction: \(\lambda\) tells us how much the maximum utility changes, not how much \(x\) or \(y\) changes.
A very common student mistake is treating \(\lambda\) as the price of good \(x\) or good \(y\). It is not a market price; it is an implicit, shadow value that exists only because the constraint binds. If the constraint does not bind — for instance, income is so high we cannot spend it all — then \(\lambda=0\). Extra income brings zero additional utility.

title: Lagrange Multipliers: The Hidden Shadow Prices Behind Constrained Optimization
text:
A numerical example
Imagine utility is Cobb‑Douglas: \(U(x,y)=x^{0.5}y^{0.5}\), prices \(p_x=p_y=1\), and initial income \(I=10\). Solving the optimization gives optimal consumption \(x^*=5\), \(y^*=5\), maximized utility \(U^*=5\), and multiplier \(\lambda^*=0.5\).
What does \(\lambda^*=0.5\) mean? If we increase income slightly from 10 to 11, the highest achievable utility rises to approximately 5.5. Adding one unit of income raises maximum utility by roughly 0.5 — matching our multiplier value. This is our shadow price: it values the constraint itself, not just the goods.

title: Lagrange Multipliers: The Hidden Shadow Prices Behind Constrained Optimization
section: Where it shows up in economics
text:
Where it shows up in economics
This shadow‑price insight extends far beyond consumer theory. A firm maximizing output subject to a cost constraint: \(\lambda\) is the marginal product of an extra dollar of cost. In public economics, constrained optimization for government spending gives multipliers that measure the welfare gain from relaxing a budget restriction. Even in data science, constrained regression uses Lagrange multipliers to interpret the cost of imposing restrictions on model parameters.
In every case, the logic is the same. Whenever a resource is scarce and binding, the Lagrange multiplier tells you its marginal implicit value. Algebra solves for quantities; the multiplier gives you the economic value of scarcity itself.

title: Lagrange Multipliers: The Hidden Shadow Prices Behind Constrained Optimization
text:
Key Takeaway
Do not view the Lagrange multiplier \(\lambda\) as just a calculus hack. When a constraint binds, it is a shadow price: it tells you how much your best possible outcome improves if you get a tiny bit more of your constrained resource. Whenever you compute a Lagrange multiplier, pause and ask: What resource is being constrained, and what is its marginal value here?

title: The Evolution of Working Hours in the United States, 2015–2025
text:
This blog asks:

How did usual weekly working hours change among U.S. workers between 2015 and 2025, and how did these changes differ across educational attainment groups?

Working hours are an economically meaningful measure of labor-market behavior. Changes in hours can reflect changes in labor demand, employment arrangements, worker preferences, and the composition of the workforce. Education is especially relevant because workers with different levels of educational attainment tend to sort into different occupations and industries, which can generate systematic differences in hours worked.
The analysis therefore focuses on two related questions:

How did the average U.S. workweek evolve from 2015 to 2025?
Did the evolution of working hours differ across educational attainment groups?

The goal is descriptive rather than causal. The figures document patterns in the CPS data; they do not identify the causal effect of any particular policy, recession, industry shock, or other event.

title: The Evolution of Working Hours in the United States, 2015–2025
text:
Data source
The data come from the IPUMS Current Population Survey (CPS) Annual Social and Economic Supplement (ASEC). I use the March ASEC sample consistently from 2015 through 2025.
The key IPUMS documentation used in this analysis is:

IPUMS CPS: Sample Weights
IPUMS CPS: ASECWT
IPUMS CPS: UHRSWORK1
IPUMS CPS: EDUC
IPUMS CPS: Technical Documentation

These sources document the choice of ASEC weights, the definition of usual hours at the main job, the coding of educational attainment, and relevant CPS comparability issues.
The main outcome is UHRSWORK1, which measures the number of hours a respondent usually works per week at their main job. IPUMS codes 99 as “99 hours per week or more,” while 997 denotes hours that vary and 999 denotes not in universe. Therefore, for calculations of the average number of hours, I retain exact reported values from 0 through 98. For the separate 40-or-more-hours analysis, I include the 99+ category.
For population statistics, I use ASECWT, the person-level ASEC weight. IPUMS specifically recommends ASECWT for person-level analyses of ASEC data, while WTFINL is intended for basic monthly CPS analyses IPUMS CPS weights.
Educational attainment is measured using the IPUMS EDUC variable. IPUMS recommends using the first two digits of EDUC for comparability across time. I group respondents into four broad categories: less than high school, high school graduate, some college, and bachelor’s degree or higher.

title: The Evolution of Working Hours in the United States, 2015–2025
text:
Why March ASEC?
The extract contains both monthly CPS observations and ASEC observations. A consistent annual comparison requires using the same type of sample and the same weight in every year. Because ASECWT is an ASEC-specific person weight, this analysis uses the March ASEC consistently rather than mixing monthly CPS observations with ASEC observations.
This choice also avoids the problem encountered when using WTFINL on this extract: the Basic Monthly weight is not available for the March ASEC observations in the earlier years in the same way needed for this analysis. The resulting sample is therefore defined consistently across all years.
The following code reads the IPUMS extract, verifies that the required variables are present, and creates the analysis sample.
The figures below are all calculated from the same cps_analysis object.

title: The Evolution of Working Hours in the United States, 2015–2025
section: Figure 1: Overall Evolution of Working Hours
text:
Figure 1: Overall Evolution of Working Hours



figure 1


The overall series shows a clear change in the level of reported usual weekly hours between 2016 and 2017. After that increase, the series is relatively stable through 2022, followed by a moderate decline in 2023 and 2024.
The endpoint values are approximately 35.9 hours in 2015 and 38.0 hours in 2025, a net change of about +2.1 hours per week.
The important economic point is that the 2015–2025 period is not characterized by a smooth linear trend. Instead, most of the visible movement occurs in particular parts of the period, especially the sharp increase around 2017 and the decline after 2022.
The 2016–2017 discontinuity should be interpreted cautiously. IPUMS documentation notes changes in CPS ASEC processing around the 2017–2019 period and advises caution when comparing affected estimates with later ASEC files. Therefore, the jump is an observed feature of the series, not evidence by itself of a causal economic shock.

text:
Figure 2: Differences Across Educational Attainment



figure 2


Figure 2 reveals a persistent education gradient in usual weekly working hours. Workers with a bachelor’s degree or higher generally report the longest usual workweeks, while workers with less than a high school education report the shortest.
The ordering is important because it is present throughout the period rather than appearing only in one year. The figure therefore suggests that educational attainment is associated with systematic differences in the amount of usual weekly labor supplied.
The changes are also not identical across groups. For example, the increase between 2015 and 2025 is much larger for workers with a high school diploma or some college than for workers with less than high school education. This means that looking only at the national average would conceal meaningful heterogeneity across education groups.
These differences should still be interpreted as descriptive associations. Education is correlated with occupation, industry, age, labor-force attachment, and other characteristics, so this figure does not identify a causal effect of education on working hours.

title: The Evolution of Working Hours in the United States, 2015–2025
section: Figure 3: How Much Did Each Education Group Change?
text:
Figure 3: How Much Did Each Education Group Change?



figure 3


Figure 3 provides a more direct comparison of the endpoints. The horizontal distance between the two dots represents the change in usual weekly hours for each education group.
The figure shows that the increase from 2015 to 2025 is not uniform. The largest endpoint increase occurs among high school graduates, followed by workers with some college and workers with a bachelor’s degree or higher. The change among workers with less than a high school education is comparatively small.
This is economically informative because the national average can remain relatively stable even when the distribution of hours changes substantially across groups. The endpoint comparison makes that heterogeneity immediately visible.

title: The Evolution of Working Hours in the United States, 2015–2025
section: Figure 4: The Education Gap in Working Hours
text:
Figure 4: The Education Gap in Working Hours



figure 4


Figure 4 summarizes the gap between the highest and lowest education groups.
The gap is approximately 6.9 hours per week in 2015 and 7.0 hours in 2025. Thus, despite changes in the individual group averages, the difference between these two education groups remains substantial throughout the sample period.
This provides a useful inequality-style perspective on the labor market. The relevant economic question is not only whether average hours changed, but also whether the distribution of work time became more or less differentiated across groups.
The figure does not establish why the gap exists. A complete explanation would require controls for occupation, industry, age, gender, family structure, and other labor-market characteristics.

text:
Figure 5: Which Years Drive the Change?



figure 5


Figure 5 decomposes the overall trend into annual changes. The largest positive change occurs in 2017, while the largest negative change occurs in 2024.
This graph adds information that Figure 1 cannot provide as directly. Figure 1 shows the level of working hours over time, whereas Figure 5 identifies the years in which the level changed most strongly.
The economic interpretation should again remain descriptive. A large year-to-year change tells us when the measured workweek moved, but not what caused that movement.

section: Figure 6: Share of Workers Working 40 or More Hours
text:
Figure 6: Share of Workers Working 40 or More Hours



figure 6


Figure 6 provides a complementary distributional measure. Instead of asking how many hours the average worker reports, it asks what share of workers report a usual workweek of at least 40 hours.
The pattern is consistent with the mean-hours results but adds information about the distribution. In 2015, the share working at least 40 hours ranges from roughly 56% among workers with less than a high school education to 76% among workers with a bachelor’s degree or higher. By 2025, the corresponding shares are approximately 56% and 82%.
The education gradient is therefore visible not only in average hours but also in the prevalence of 40-or-more-hour workweeks. This makes the result less dependent on a single mean and suggests that the education differences extend to the distribution of weekly work time.

title: Where Are America’s Industries, and What Do They Mean for Local Economies?
text:
Across the United States, counties differ widely in the industries that support their local economies. How does a county’s industrial structure relate to its economy and population?
To answer that question, this analysis maps major industries across U.S. counties and examines how industrial specialization is associated with employment, wages, household income, population, and educational attainment—and how these patterns have changed over time.
Using county-level data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics’ Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) and the Census Bureau’s American Community Survey (ACS), this study combines GIS maps, location quotients, and descriptive comparisons to explore these relationships.

title: Where Industries Thrive: Mapping Jobs, Income, and Regional Economic Change in the United States
text:
Three sources, three perspectives
The analysis combines three public data sources.

Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW), U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics: annual-average employment by county and industry.
American Community Survey (ACS), U.S. Census Bureau: median household income, labor-force characteristics, and educational attainment.
TIGER/Line county boundaries, U.S. Census Bureau: geographic boundaries used to map county-level measures.

QCEW measures jobs by place of work. ACS household income and labor-market characteristics describe residents. The two sources complement each other, but they do not measure exactly the same population.
For the historical comparison, 2019 and 2024 QCEW annual averages are used. ACS data are taken from the 2019 and 2024 five-year estimates. These ACS estimates cover 2015–2019 and 2020–2024, respectively; they are not single-year snapshots.

title: Where Industries Thrive: Mapping Jobs, Income, and Regional Economic Change in the United States
text:
A fair comparison across counties
A county with 20,000 manufacturing jobs might be a major manufacturing center—or it might simply be a large county with many jobs in every industry. Raw employment counts cannot distinguish these situations.
The analysis therefore uses the location quotient (LQ):
[ LQ_{c,i} = {E_{US,i}/E_{US}} ]
where (E_{c,i}) is employment in industry (i) in county (c), and (E_c) is total employment in that county. The national terms are defined in the same way.

(LQ=1): the industry’s share of county employment equals its national share.
(LQ>1): the industry is more concentrated locally than nationally.
(LQ<1): the industry represents a smaller share of local employment than it does nationally.

An LQ of 2 does not mean twice as many jobs or twice the productivity. It means the industry’s share of local employment is twice the corresponding national share.

title: Where Industries Thrive: Mapping Jobs, Income, and Regional Economic Change in the United States
text:
What counts as technology-related employment?
“High tech” is not one industry code. To make the comparison transparent, this article uses three selected NAICS industries:

51: Information
334: Computer and electronic product manufacturing
5415: Computer systems design and related services

This is a practical proxy, not a complete or official definition of high-tech employment. It omits technology workers employed in industries such as finance, health care, and retail. The selected categories avoid adding broad parent industries to their own subindustries, which would double-count employment.

title: Where Industries Thrive: Mapping Jobs, Income, and Regional Economic Change in the United States
text:
Download QCEW annual averages
QCEW annual-average single files are available from the official BLS download system. The following code downloads the 2019 and 2024 CSV archives directly. The files are read into R without requiring separate scripts or manually maintained intermediate data files.

title: Where Industries Thrive: Mapping Jobs, Income, and Regional Economic Change in the United States
text:
Calculate industry concentration
The denominator must use the same ownership and industry coverage as the numerator. Here, county and national totals both use QCEW private-sector all-industry employment.
Missing or suppressed employment is kept as missing. It is never converted to zero.

title: Where Industries Thrive: Mapping Jobs, Income, and Regional Economic Change in the United States
text:
Data sources

U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, QCEW downloadable data files.
U.S. Census Bureau, 2024 ACS five-year estimates.
U.S. Census Bureau, TIGER/Line Shapefiles.

title: Where Industries Thrive: Mapping Jobs, Income, and Regional Economic Change in the United States
text:
Limitations

This is a county-level descriptive analysis, not a causal study.
QCEW employment is measured by workplace; ACS household and labor-market measures describe residents.
The technology-related employment measure is a selected-industry proxy, not a comprehensive definition of high-tech activity.
QCEW suppression and missing values can affect county-industry observations. Missing values are not interpreted as zero.
ACS 2019 and 2024 five-year estimates describe different five-year periods, not single-year snapshots.
The 2019–2024 comparison includes the pandemic shock and recovery. It cannot isolate the effects of technology, trade, or industrial policy.

The central takeaway is simple: where jobs are concentrated matters, but specialization alone does not tell us whether a local economy is prosperous, inclusive, or resilient. GIS helps identify the patterns. Understanding them requires combining geography with careful economic reasoning.

title: Where Are America’s Industries, and What Do They Mean for Local Economies?
text:
This analysis combines two public data sources:

Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW): annual-average covered employment and average weekly wages by county and industry.
U.S. Census Bureau, American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year estimates: population, labor-force measures, median household income, and educational attainment.

County boundaries are obtained from Census TIGER/Line geography through the tigris R package.
The 2019 and 2024 ACS 5-year estimates describe the periods 2015–2019 and 2020–2024, respectively. They are not single-year snapshots.
QCEW measures jobs by workplace, while ACS describes people by residence. QCEW average weekly wages are not equivalent to household income. Residents may commute to other counties, and household income also depends on household composition, hours worked, and non-labor income.
QCEW does not comprehensively cover agricultural employment. Accordingly, the broad industry maps focus on the major QCEW sectors available in the downloaded county files rather than claiming to represent every industry in the economy.

title: Where Are America’s Industries, and What Do They Mean for Local Economies?
text:
1.1 The broad industrial landscape
These county-level maps show each major industry’s share of private-sector jobs in 2024, revealing sharply different geographic footprints. Trade and construction appear broadly nationwide, while education-health jobs anchor many small rural counties. Manufacturing concentrates in the Midwest and South. Information, finance and professional services cluster in large metro areas, and resource extraction only lights up resource-rich counties. Note that high employment share can reflect tiny total jobs in sparse rural counties.





Selected major industries as a share of county private-sector employment, 2024.

title: Where Are America’s Industries, and What Do They Mean for Local Economies?
section: 1.2 Two case studies: manufacturing and professional services
text:
1.2 Two case studies: manufacturing and professional services
Manufacturing builds physical goods and sustains sprawling supply chains, often tied to community debates about good local jobs. Professional and business services include consulting and technical work that powers modern firms. This analysis single out these sectors for comparison as they stand for two currently vital economic paths: goods production and knowledge work. Their contrasting geographic clusters create a natural lens to investigate whether industry specialization translates into better economic outcomes for county residents.
A location quotient (LQ) compares an industry’s share of local private employment with its share of national private employment:
\(LQ_{ic} =\frac{\text{Industry employment}_{ic}/\text{Private employment}_{c}}{\text{National industry employment}_{i}/\text{National private employment}}\)
An LQ above 1 means that the industry represents a larger share of local employment than it does nationally. It does not necessarily indicate a large absolute number of jobs or higher productivity.





County unemployment rates, ACS 2020–2024 5-year estimates.









County employment-population ratios, ACS 2020–2024 5-year estimates.




Manufacturing specialization while professional‑business services cluster heavily in major metro areas. Counties with manufacturing specialization are scattered across the Midwest and rural South,concentrating across many non‑metropolitan counties. Professional-business services specialization, cluster heavily in major metro areas. High LQ signals local job concentration in that industry.

title: Where Are America’s Industries, and What Do They Mean for Local Economies?
section: 2.1 Does manufacturing specialization correspond to higher household income?
text:
2.1 Does manufacturing specialization correspond to higher household income?





Manufacturing specialization and median household income, 2024.




This scatter plot compares counties’ manufacturing location quotient to resident median household income. A modest manufacturing presence can support household incomes by supplying solid blue-collar work. But counties overly specialized in manufacturing face risks from sectoral shocks and limited alternative job opportunities, so income no longer rises and may even fall. The scattered points show manufacturing jobs alone cannot determine residents’ prosperity. Because workers commute across county boundaries, factory job concentration does not guarantee local households capture the economic gains from that industrial activity.

title: Where Are America’s Industries, and What Do They Mean for Local Economies?
section: 2.2 How do average weekly wages differ across sectors?
text:
2.2 How do average weekly wages differ across sectors?





County-level average weekly wages in manufacturing and professional/business services, 2024.




Are professional service jobs consistently better paid than manufacturing roles? This graph compares county average weekly wages across the two sectors. Professional and business services have a higher typical county wage, rewarding specialized technical and analytical skills. But wages vary widely within each sector from county to county. Remember these figures are county averages, hiding big gaps between individual workers. Industry sets the baseline for pay, yet local economic conditions also shape what workers ultimately earn.

title: Where Are America’s Industries, and What Do They Mean for Local Economies?
section: 2.3 Where are labor-market conditions stronger or weaker?
text:
2.3 Where are labor-market conditions stronger or weaker?





County unemployment rate and employment-population ratio, ACS 2020–2024 5-year estimates.







County unemployment rate and employment-population ratio, ACS 2020–2024 5-year estimates.




These two maps show clear regional disparities tied to local industry composition. Counties with strong professional and business services tend to display low unemployment and high employment-population ratios, reflecting abundant skilled work. Many rural counties reliant on manufacturing or resource industries often see elevated unemployment and weaker adult employment rates. Some tourism-dependent counties show volatile labor outcomes. This reveals that the industrial footprint we mapped earlier shapes residents’ job prospects as the mix of local jobs determines both unemployment levels and broader workforce participation.

title: Where Are America’s Industries, and What Do They Mean for Local Economies?
text:
3.1 Population change





Percent difference in county population between the 2015–2019 and 2020–2024 ACS 5-year estimates.




Counties with expanding professional and business services often see population gains, as knowledge jobs draw working-age households. Many rural manufacturing counties face population losses, because shrinking factory employment reduces the region’s pull. Red regions lose residents while blue regions grow. Please note that these percentage changes combine migration, births and deaths and they cannot be attributed solely to people moving for jobs.

title: Where Are America’s Industries, and What Do They Mean for Local Economies?
text:
3.2 Educational attainment and industrial specialization





Educational attainment and manufacturing/professional-services specialization, 2024.




This scatterplot visualizes the mutual attraction between educated workers and local industries. The rising blue trend line for professional and business services shows that counties with more college graduates become increasingly specialized in knowledge-intensive work: the industry draws educated talent, and this talent in turn supports further industry growth. Manufacturing’s red inverted-U curve tells a different story. Manufacturing specialization peaks at moderate bachelor-degree shares; in counties with very high educational attainment, manufacturing location quotients decline, as highly educated residents tend not to cluster in manufacturing-specialized regions.

title: Where Are America’s Industries, and What Do They Mean for Local Economies?
text:
4.1 Manufacturing employment change





Percent change in manufacturing employment between 2019 and 2024.




This county-level map reveals uneven shifts in manufacturing employment from 2019 to 2024. Parts of the traditional industrial heartland experienced manufacturing job losses, while scattered counties across the South and some western regions saw manufacturing employment expand. These divergent outcomes reshape regional industrial attractiveness: areas losing factory jobs become less appealing to production workers, while counties gaining manufacturing work draw residents seeking blue-collar roles.

title: Where Are America’s Industries, and What Do They Mean for Local Economies?
section: 4.2 Do manufacturing and professional services grow in the same places?
text:
4.2 Do manufacturing and professional services grow in the same places?





County employment growth in manufacturing and professional/business services, 2019–2024.




A minority of counties expand employment in both industries. More commonly, growth happens in only one sector: some counties gain manufacturing jobs without professional service growth, while others expand professional services with weak manufacturing performance. Some counties lose jobs in both sectors. These varied trajectories reveal the two industries favor different locations and draw different worker groups. (This metric only records net change and cannot isolate pandemic or policy effects.)

title: Where Are America’s Industries, and What Do They Mean for Local Economies?
section: What this analysis can—and cannot—tell us
text:
What this analysis can—and cannot—tell us
This project is a descriptive county-level analysis. It does not establish that industrial specialization causes differences in income, education, unemployment, or population change.
Important limitations include:

QCEW measures covered jobs by workplace. It is not a complete census of all forms of work, and some county-industry estimates may be unavailable or suppressed.
ACS measures residents. Residents may commute to jobs in other counties.
Weekly wages are not household income. The measures have different units, populations, and denominators.
Educational attainment is not a direct skill measure. A bachelor’s-degree share is one indicator of formal education.
Population change is not net migration. Births, deaths, migration, and estimation uncertainty all contribute.
ACS 5-year estimates are multi-year estimates. The 2019 and 2024 values describe 2015–2019 and 2020–2024.
Associations are not causal effects. Urbanization, demographics, cost of living, commuting, and other factors may influence the observed patterns.

title: Where Are America’s Industries, and What Do They Mean for Local Economies?
text:
Final takeaway
There is no single map that can label a county’s economy as successful or unsuccessful. Manufacturing, professional services, health care, logistics, construction, finance, and other industries play different roles in different places.
A clearer picture emerges when we examine industrial composition alongside workplace wages, resident income, labor-market conditions, population, educational attainment, and employment change.
For residents and policymakers, the practical question is not simply “Which industry is best?” It is:
What kinds of jobs are available locally, who can access them, how are they paid, and how is the local mix of opportunities changing?

title: Where Are America’s Industries, and What Do They Mean for Local Economies?
text:
When we talk about local economies, it is tempting to judge a county’s prosperity by its dominant industry. We often assume manufacturing‑heavy places will have higher household incomes, or that service‑sector hubs automatically deliver broad‑based prosperity. But industrial job concentration does not guarantee better living standards for local residents.
This leads to a broader economic question: How is local industrial structure associated with employment, wages, household income, population, and educational attainment across U.S. counties?
This analysis draws on two core public datasets. The BLS Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) records private‑sector jobs and weekly wages by workplace at the county‑industry level. The U.S. Census American Community Survey (ACS) 5‑year estimates report resident‑side outcomes: household income, unemployment, population and educational attainment.
A critical distinction matters: QCEW measures where jobs are located, while ACS measures where people live. Many workers commute across county borders. Industry weekly wages are not household income, and ACS multi‑year estimates pool survey responses rather than representing single‑year snapshots. This work is descriptive, not causal: it uncovers geographic associations but cannot prove industry specialization causes income or labor‑market outcomes.

title: Where Are America’s Industries, and What Do They Mean for Local Economies?
text:
Sources and reproducibility

U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages.
U.S. Census Bureau, American Community Survey.
U.S. Census Bureau, TIGER/Line Shapefiles.

The code in this document downloads QCEW annual files, retrieves ACS 5‑year county estimates, joins them to county boundaries, and creates the figures. It requires the R packages listed in the setup chunk and a Census API key stored privately in ~/.Renviron.
The code checks key columns, expected industry codes, and duplicate county‑sector records. If the downloaded QCEW file does not match the expected structure, inspect its actual codes and verify the mapping before interpreting the figures.

title: Where Are America’s Industries, and What Do They Mean for Local Economies?
text:
5.1 Key Takeaways

Specialization is not prosperity: A high location quotient indicates relative industry concentration, not necessarily more jobs or higher household income.
Employment, wages, and income measure different things: Workplace-based job and wage data do not directly capture residents’ financial well-being.
People and industries vary across regions: Population trends, educational attainment, and labor-market conditions provide important context for local economies.
Regional growth is uneven: Manufacturing and professional and business services follow different employment trajectories across counties.

For residents and policymakers, understanding a local economy means asking not only which industries dominate, but also what jobs are available, how they are paid, who benefits, and how opportunities change over time.
For residents and policymakers, the practical question is not simply “Which industry is best?” It is: What kinds of jobs are available locally, who can access them, how are they paid, and how is the local mix of opportunities changing?

title: Are Household Incomes Keeping Up With Grocery Prices?
section: A higher grocery bill is not the same as a higher relative price
text:
A higher grocery bill is not the same as a higher relative price
Figure 1 measures the food-at-home CPI divided by the all-items CPI, normalized to 100 in 2015:
\[
R_t=100\frac{F_t/A_t}{F_{2015}/A_{2015}}.
\]
Here, \(F_t\) and \(A_t\) are annual-average price indexes. A rise means groceries became more expensive relative to the broad consumer basket, which itself includes food. This ratio measures relative price movements, not the dollar price of one basket compared with another.








Figure 1: Food prices relative to the overall consumer basket. Source: BLS; annual averages and author calculations. Acquisition source recorded in saved metadata.





From 2015 to 2024, grocery prices increased by 26.5%, while overall prices increased by 32.4%. Consequently, the relative food-price ratio decreased by 4.4%. Over 2020–2024, that same ratio increased by 1.1%. The post-2020 experience therefore cannot stand in for the full decade. Changing an index’s normalization rescales the line; changing the comparison’s starting year changes the economic question. Percentage changes in the ratio between fixed endpoints are independent of normalization.

title: Are Household Incomes Keeping Up With Grocery Prices?
section: Slower inflation does not restore earlier prices
text:
Slower inflation does not restore earlier prices








Figure 2: Monthly food-at-home inflation: 100 times the change from the same month a year earlier. Source: BLS. Acquisition source recorded in saved metadata.





Food inflation peaked at 13.6% in 八月 2022 within this sample. Its subsequent decline describes disinflation: prices rose more slowly. Only a negative rate indicates falling prices relative to a year earlier. A lower inflation rate can therefore coexist with grocery bills well above their pre-surge levels.

title: Are Household Incomes Keeping Up With Grocery Prices?
section: The grocery basket contains different price experiences
text:
The grocery basket contains different price experiences








Figure 3: Cumulative changes in annual-average prices, 2015–2024, for five selected categories. These are not contributions to aggregate inflation. Source: BLS. Acquisition source recorded in saved metadata.





Across these categories, cumulative increases range from 20.1% to 31.3%. Households buying different baskets can experience different pressures. These bars are unweighted category price changes, so they cannot identify which category contributed most to aggregate food inflation. Doing that would require expenditure weights.

title: Are Household Incomes Keeping Up With Grocery Prices?
section: How much food could median household income buy?
text:
How much food could median household income buy?
I deflate nominal median household income by the food CPI and normalize the resulting ratio to 100 in 2015. Using an already inflation-adjusted income series would adjust for prices twice.
\[
P_t=100\frac{Y_t/F_t}{Y_{2015}/F_{2015}}.
\]








Figure 4: Median household income deflated by the food-at-home CPI, 2015 = 100. Source: Census and BLS; author calculations. Acquisition source recorded in saved metadata.





Food purchasing power increased by 16.3% over 2015–2024, compared with decreased by 0.2% over 2020–2024. This is a descriptive benchmark, not a paycheck measure or a household budget: household income includes sources beyond wages, and households differ in size, expenses, and income growth. The median can also change as household composition changes. These aggregates cannot establish that every household recovered, or that any loss was permanent or temporary beyond 2024.

title: Are Household Incomes Keeping Up With Grocery Prices?
text:
Data sources and replication
Series definitions: food CPI, overall CPI, and nominal median household income. Official fallback sources: BLS Public Data API and Census historical household income, Table H-5. Category IDs and actual download URLs are recorded in the accompanying README and metadata. Historical data may be revised; the saved files define the replicated snapshot. See replication instructions. All analysis and figure-generation code is included in this QMD.
